passage: Public institutions depend on trust. Trust does not mean that citizens agree with every decision. It means they believe decisions are made through fair procedures, relevant evidence and accountable processes. When an agency explains why a policy was adopted and publishes information about its performance, citizens can judge it more intelligently. Transparency therefore supports, rather than replaces, responsibility. A transparent institution may still make mistakes, but it makes correction easier because errors can be identified and discussed. In this sense, public trust is strengthened not by claiming perfection but by demonstrating openness and willingness to learn.

passage: A city may widen roads to reduce congestion, but road expansion alone does not always solve the problem. A city that evaluates only the immediate increase in road capacity may overlook changes in demand that occur later.

solution.passage: Reliable statistics are essential for public policy, but numbers do not speak entirely for themselves. A percentage can be technically correct while creating a misleading impression if the denominator is unclear or the comparison period changes. Policymakers should therefore ask what was measured, how it was measured and against what baseline. Graphs and summaries can help communicate trends, but they should not replace examination of the underlying data. Statistical literacy is valuable not only for researchers but also for citizens who need to assess claims made in public debate.

solution.passage: Scientific findings become useful to society when they can be communicated clearly and applied responsibly. A study may produce an interesting result, but one study rarely settles a complex question by itself. Replication, comparison with other evidence and careful interpretation help determine how much confidence should be placed in a finding. Public communication also matters: overstating uncertain results can create unrealistic expectations, while excessive technical language can prevent people from understanding important conclusions. Good science communication therefore requires both accuracy and clarity.

solution.passage: Public budgets are choices among competing priorities. When a government increases spending on one programme, it may have fewer resources available for another unless revenue also increases. This does not mean that every spending decision is a zero-sum choice: productive investment may generate future benefits or revenue. Nevertheless, budget analysis should identify the opportunity cost of major decisions. Asking what alternative use of funds is being forgone helps decision-makers compare programmes more realistically and explain priorities to the public.
